## Overview

Spraying a field selects for resistance in its pests; refuges that are not
sprayed, and pests that move between fields, slow that down. @Peck1997 asked
how the economic threshold at which farmers spray, the life history of the
pest and the arrangement of a region change the time until resistance takes
over. Their model is a lattice of fields:

- each field holds a pest population with one resistance gene, which grows
  logistically each generation;
- resistance costs its carriers a little;
- a treated field whose population passes the economic threshold is sprayed,
  and the spray kills susceptible pests (and some heterozygotes);
- a share of every field's pests then moves to the neighbouring fields;
- refuges are never sprayed, and rotated fields are emptied every other
  generation.

After a random start, the model is deterministic. This implementation is an
**adaptation**: it follows the source's equations, choosing where they are
ambiguous as the deviations below list.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## A single field

The source first studied one field: 10⁷ pests, a carrying capacity twice that,
a resistance allele starting at a frequency of 0.0005, a spray killing 75% of
susceptibles, a cost of 0.0005 and a dominance of 0.05. A field on its own is
a lattice of one cell.

```{julia}
model = build_resistance_regional()
function single(; r=1.5, delta=0.5)
    u0 = (; N=fill(1e7, 1, 1), q=fill(5e-4, 1, 1), sprayed=fill(true, 1, 1),
          rotated=fill(false, 1, 1), K=fill(2e7, 1, 1), neighbours=fill(Int8(0), 1, 1))
    p = merge(defaults(model), (; r, delta, rho=0.75, s=5e-4, h=0.05, Ks=2e7))
    t = resistance_time(solve(CAProblem(model, u0, 250, p; space=Grid(1, 1))))
    return t === nothing ? 250 : t
end
deltas = 0:0.02:1
rs = 0.2:0.05:4
plot(plot(deltas, [single(; delta=d) for d in deltas]; xlabel="threshold δ (share of K)",
          title="r = 1.5"),
     plot(rs, [single(; r) for r in rs]; xlabel="growth rate r", title="δ = 0.5");
     ylabel="time to resistance (generations)", legend=false, lw=2, layout=(1, 2),
     size=(850, 330), titlefontsize=10, left_margin=4Plots.mm, bottom_margin=4Plots.mm)
```

As in the source's Fig. 2, a higher threshold (spraying less often) delays
resistance in steps, from about 58 generations at δ = 0.2 to 110 at δ = 1, and
faster growth hastens it: about 216 generations at r = 0.35, 90 at r = 1 and
37 at r = 3.5. The steps come from the population's cycles: as the threshold
rises, the cycle sprays in fewer generations. Spraying every generation
(δ = 0) gives 37 generations, against about 50 in the source.

## A region

The source's spatial runs use 50 × 50 fields, 55% of them treated, with half
the treated fields' carrying capacity in the refuges. With half of each
field's pests migrating each generation (the source's Fig. 6), resistance
spreads in patches:

```{julia}
prob = problem(:resistance_regional; seed=1, pmap=(; s=0.005, delta=0.8, M=0.5))
sol = solve(prob)
println("time to resistance: ", resistance_time(sol))
plot([heatmap(sol.u[t + 1].q; clims=(0, 1), c=cgrad(:grays; rev=true), yflip=true, colorbar=false,
              title="t = $t", titlefontsize=9, ticks=false, aspect_ratio=1)
      for t in (57, 63, 69, 75, 81, 87)]...; layout=(2, 3), size=(800, 540))
```

Dark fields are resistant. Patches appear after about 60 generations, grow
and merge, and cover most of the region by generation 87; resistance takes
over the region (a mean frequency above one half) at generation 81. The
patches cut across the map of treated fields and refuges: what makes a field
resistant is as much its neighbours as its own spraying.

## Migration and refuges

The source's Fig. 7 compares migration of 0.5%, 5% and 50% a generation with
95% and 55% of fields treated. Here each region is shown when its mean
frequency first passes 0.3:

```{julia}
snap = Matrix{Any}(undef, 2, 3)
for (i, lambda) in enumerate((0.95, 0.55)), (j, M) in enumerate((0.005, 0.05, 0.5))
    s = solve(problem(:resistance_regional; lambda, kappa=0.9, seed=3,
                      pmap=(; M, delta=0.45)))
    k = something(findfirst(u -> resistance_summary(u).mean > 0.3, s.u), length(s.u))
    snap[i, j] = heatmap(s.u[k].q; clims=(0, 1), c=cgrad(:grays; rev=true), yflip=true, colorbar=false,
                         ticks=false, aspect_ratio=1, titlefontsize=8,
                         title="λ = $lambda, M = $(100M)%, t = $(k - 1)")
end
plot(permutedims(snap)...; layout=(2, 3), size=(800, 560))
```

With little migration each field follows its own spraying: with 95% of fields
treated, the refuges stay susceptible on their own at 0.5% migration and with
their neighbours, in small crosses, at 5%; with 55% treated, susceptible and
resistant fields form a fine mosaic. With much migration, resistance forms
large smooth patches that ignore the spray map.

## The factorial

The source ran every combination of the levels of its Table 2 and averaged the
time to resistance over the others. All 41,472 runs of that factorial, one
for each combination:

```{julia}
levels = (q0=(5e-4, 5e-3), N0=(1e6, 1e8), r=(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5), h=(0.05, 0.35, 0.65),
          k=(2, 3), kappa=(0.3, 0.6, 0.9), delta=(0.1, 0.45, 0.8), rho=(0.55, 0.95),
          s=(5e-4, 5e-3), lambda=(0.55, 0.95), psi=(0.0, 0.4), M=(0.005, 0.05, 0.5))
combos = vec(collect(Iterators.product(values(levels)...)))
T = zeros(length(combos))
moran = fill(NaN, length(combos))
Threads.@threads for i in eachindex(combos)
    c = NamedTuple{keys(levels)}(combos[i])
    integ = init(problem(:resistance_regional; N0=c.N0, k=c.k, kappa=c.kappa, q0=c.q0,
                         lambda=c.lambda, psi=c.psi, seed=i,
                         pmap=(; r=c.r, h=c.h, delta=c.delta, rho=c.rho, s=c.s, M=c.M));
                 save_everystep=false)
    T[i] = 250
    for t in 1:250
        step!(integ)
        sm = resistance_summary(integ.u)
        if sm.mean > 0.5
            T[i], moran[i] = t, sm.morans_i
            break
        end
    end
end
level(n) = [c[findfirst(==(n), keys(levels))] for c in combos]
[(; factor=n, levels=levels[n],
  mean_time=[round(mean(T[level(n) .== v]); digits=1) for v in levels[n]])
 for n in (:r, :h, :delta, :M, :psi, :lambda)]
```

As in the source's Fig. 3, faster growth and more dominant resistance hasten
resistance most, and a higher threshold and more migration delay it. The
correlations of the time to resistance with the parameters follow the source's
Table 3:

```{julia}
[(; factor=n, correlation=round(cor(Float64.(level(n)), T); digits=3))
 for n in (:h, :r, :rho, :q0, :lambda, :M, :delta, :kappa, :psi, :s, :N0)]
```

and the spatial autocorrelation of resistance when it takes over rises with
migration, as in its Fig. 5:

```{julia}
[(; M=m, morans_i=round(mean(filter(!isnan, moran[level(:M) .== m])); digits=2))
 for m in levels.M]
```

One result is not reproduced: in the source, rotating 40% of the fields
delays resistance by about 20 generations when migration is low, which makes
the main effect of migration fall and then rise. Here rotation changes little
at low migration; the source does not say which fields rotate or when in the
generation they are emptied.
